articles.title: Woman Unknown review – postwar paranoia with some deliciously dastardly Du Maurier touches
articles.summary: Venice film festival A nanny becomes the new lady of a prosperous Copenhagen house as accused Nazi sympathisers are violently shamed in May el-Toukhy’s shrewd, painful portrait of survival.
body: Here is an elegantly appointed drama-thriller from May el-Toukhy, about sexual shame and political paranoia in postwar Denmark, with something of Alfred Hitchcock’s Rebecca, which it consciously recalls. As director and co-writer, El-Toukhy has created a shrewd and painful movie about the terrible things you need to do to survive, and what it takes to forget those things afterwards.

The scene is a prosperous, upper-middle-class apartment in Copenhagen just after the second world war, when the Danish resistance was permitted the powers of a secret-police militia to detain and interrogate those suspected of having given assistance to the Nazis. Christian (Carsten Bjørnlund) is a ageing factory owner and widower who has evidently fallen in love with his infant daughter’s nanny: this is Marie (fiercely and convincingly played by Mathilde Arcel). Or at any rate, he sees that the child needs a new mother, finds Marie attractive and appreciates her submissive attitude. They are now engaged.
points: Venice film festival A nanny becomes the new lady of a prosperous Copenhagen house as accused Nazi sympathisers are violently shamed in May el-Toukhy’s shrewd, painful portrait of survival.

articles.title: Cult of male genius holding female film-makers back, says Woman Unknown director
articles.summary: May el-Toukhy says we must end veneration of male directors that causes ‘structural problem’ for women. The enduring cult of male genius is keeping down female film-makers, one of the only two female directors in the running for the top prize at this year’s Venice film festival has warned.
body: “I’ve never ever read an article where a female director is promoted as a genius,” said the Danish-Egyptian director May el-Toukhy, whose film Woman Unknown has been selected for the Golden Lion competition on the Lido this year.
“It’s not that I think I am one, but it’s just interesting that this is so systemic,” she added. “All of us are responsible for changing that discourse.”

El-Toukhy’s post-second world war period drama was the only film by a woman in the main competition when the line-up was announced in July. Since then, the festival directors have added the documentary NAZA, which is co-directed by Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor and produced by the Guardian.
A competition prize at Europe’s top festivals, Cannes, Venice and Berlin, is seen as a major door-opener for films seeking distribution deals around the world.
points: May el-Toukhy says we must end veneration of male directors that causes ‘structural problem’ for women.

body: Will the newsroom drama be this year’s “One Night in Miami” or can it go further in the awards race with Jack O’Connell and Pearce?
The central question is not simply how Murdoch built a newspaper. It is how two men helped invent the modern attention economy that shapes all of our lives today.

Guy Pearce plays a brash, thirty-something Murdoch, an outsider with a chip on his shoulder and a plan for disrupting Fleet Street. Jack O’Connell plays editor Larry Lamb, the working-class newspaperman Murdoch pushes past every line the establishment believes cannot be crossed.
Both actors have obvious awards narratives, but two very different categories to break into.

articles.title: John Turturro Has Waited 40 Years for an Oscar Nomination. ‘The Only Living Pickpocket in New York’ Makes the Case
articles.summary: Forty years into a career that has made him one of American cinema’s most recognizable character actors, John Turturro has a Cannes best actor prize, an enviable résumé and exactly zero Oscar mornings when his name was read aloud with the words “and the nominees are.” Sony Pictures Classics is…
body: Turturro has spent four decades operating in the space reserved for actors everyone recognizes and almost nobody thinks of as an Oscar nominee. He has worked with masters of cinema such as the Coen brothers, Spike Lee and Robert Redford and has appeared opposite everyone from Tom Hanks to Adam Sandler. He’s played gangsters, professors, detectives, eccentrics, husbands, fathers and men who seem to have wandered into the wrong movie and somehow made it better.

And it’s not like he hasn’t been close. Turturro won best actor at Cannes for the Coen brothers’ “Barton Fink” in 1991. Three years later, his combustible Herbie Stempel in Robert Redford’s “Quiz Show” collected Golden Globe and SAG Award nominations, the kind of precursor support that usually precedes an Oscar bid. But each time, the industry seemed to look elsewhere.

The television world has been kinder. His weary defense attorney in “The Night Of,” HBO’s 2016 crime drama, drew Emmy, Golden Globe and SAG Award nominations. His tender, unraveling Irving Bailiff on “Severance,” Apple TV’s dystopian workplace thriller, has since earned him two Emmy nominations, the most recent lost to his own castmate Tramell Tillman in 2025.

articles.title: ‘Woman Unknown’ Review: Some More Problematic Sex — and Its Consequences — by Denmark’s May el-Toukhy
articles.summary: Against the rubble gray and stiff mahogany with which director May el-Toukhy washes out her post-Second World War Copenhagen, the pops of crimson in “Woman Unknown” announce a stark symbolism that’s about as subtle as the red swastika eventually smeared on the front door of protagonist Marie…
body: With her follow-up to 'Queen of Hearts,' the only woman director in competition at Venice unfolds a provocative but predictable psychodrama about sexual shame in post-WWII Copenhagen, anchored by a magnetic Mathilde Arcel.

Marie, a maid and nanny to the twiggy blonde child of her employer Christian (Carsten Bjornlund), a widower and owner of a glove-making factory, carries herself as if permanently bound in a corset: breath held, mouth tight, her eyes shifty as if dreading the next reprimand. It makes sense given her workplace’s exacting standards, in which place settings are arranged according to centimeter-precise measurements and stony head maid Esther (Marina Bouras) is always watching.

articles.title: Wim Wenders clarifies that he does not believe film-makers should stay out of politics
articles.summary: Director’s controversial comments earlier this year warned of films that ‘enter the field of politics’ The director Wim Wenders has clarified personal views on the relationship between cinema and politics that caused controversy earlier in the year, saying at the Venice film festival that he does…
body: During the Berlin film festival, the veteran German director, who was acting as the jury president, had said at a press conference that “we have to stay out of politics because if we make movies that are dedicatedly political, we enter the field of politics.”

The remark drew much attention amid criticism of the German government’s support of Israel over the war in Gaza, and incensed some fellow film-makers, with the Indian author Arundhati Roy calling the comments “unconscionable” and pulling out of an event in the German capital.
Asked by the Guardian at a press conference in Venice whether he stood by the comments, Wenders said he “could repeat the same thing” but conceded he “could be more explicit”.

“What I said then was, as film-makers, we are the opposite of politicians. We have empathy. Politics work without empathy; that’s all I said,” said the auteur, who had come to the Lido to present a documentary about the Swiss architect Peter Zumthor.

articles.title: Macklemore Calls Out ‘Free Palestine’ Onstage, Spurring Petition Demanding He Leave Ed Sheeran Tour
articles.summary: Macklemore opened for Ed Sheeran on Friday night in New Jersey at the MetLife Stadium, and during his set the rapper sang out “Free Palestine” before launching into a speech, telling the audience he wanted people in Gaza and the occupied West Bank to know they had not been forgotten.
body: The petition, which does not show how many signatures it has gathered, reads “This was an Ed Sheeran concert – not a political rally, not a protest, and not an activist event. The issue is not whether Macklemore has the right to hold political views. The question is where the line should be drawn when an opening act uses a global concert platform to advance a one-sided political agenda.”

Macklemore also called out U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement during his remarks. He released the song “Hind’s Hall,” which criticizes Israel’s actions in Gaza, in 2024 and has directed proceeds from the song to go to humanitarian efforts from the UNRWA.

On social media, some concertgoers said they walked out because they had not expected a ‘political rally,” accusing Macklemore of antisemitism. Others applauded his remarks, writing “Music has always been a vital platform for human rights advocacy, not just mindless escape.”

articles.title: French thriller Jupiter brings nuclear anxiety to red carpets of Venice
articles.summary: Director Alexandre Smia says film about Russia detonating nuclear warhead – and US refusing to respond – is not unrealistic. Russia has detonated a nuclear warhead over the Black Sea to underline its desire to revenge an assassination attempt on the Russian president.
body: A new thriller, which has brought nuclear anxiety to the red carpets of the Venice film festival this week, plays through what would happen next. In Jupiter, which premiered on the Lido on Friday, the duty to square up to the Kremlin and enter the stress-inducing mind games of the nuclear deterrent falls on the fictional French president Paul Archambault (played by the hulking French actor Denis Ménochet), who is backed in his mission by the British prime minister.
It’s a scenario that is far from unrealistic, the French film-maker Alexandre Smia said on the eve of his film’s premiere.

“Even if the US disengagement from Nato is not official, we have reason to doubt that the US would offer its nuclear umbrella if one European city were to be attacked nowadays,” said Smia, who has previously directed episodes of the French spy TV series Le Bureau des Légendes.

“And considering that France is the only country in Europe that is both a member of the European community, of the security council of the United Nations and of Nato, it naturally becomes actually the country where the responsibility of making decisions lies.”

articles.title: ‘Spider-Man: Brand New Day’ Topping Box Office for Sixth Weekend in a Row
articles.summary: The Spider-Man feature is soon aiming to become the top grossing movie domestically of all time, as Tom Holland's other summer movie, 'The Odyssey,' comes in at No. 2.
body: After the fireworks of the summer, the season comes to an end with a sleepy weekend at the box office, at least in terms of new entries like By Any Means and Onslaught.

Sony and Marvel’s Spider-Man: Brand New Day is expected to be No. 1 for its sixth weekend in a row, with roughly $22 million over the four-day frame. The Destin Daniel Cretton-directed feature just crossed $900 million domestically, making it only the second film ever to do so, behind 2015’s Star Wars: The Force Awakens, which stands as the all-time domestic holder at $936 million. Brand New Day should pass that record soon to become the all-time domestic leader. Globally, Brand New Day has surpassed $2.33 billion, making it the No. 3 movie of all time behind Avatar and Avengers: Endgame, after passing up Avatar: The Way of Water.

Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey, now in its eighth weekend and also starring Brand New Day star Tom Holland, will come in at at No. 2 with around $16.4 million, which would put it at $588.1 million domestically through Monday for the Universal title.
points: The Spider-Man feature is soon aiming to become the top grossing movie domestically of all time, as Tom Holland's other summer movie, 'The Odyssey,' comes in at No. 2.

articles.title: Pulp top the bill at 20th End of the Road Festival
articles.summary: The End Of The Road Festival near Blandford Forum sees a packed event with 15,000 visitors.
body: A sell-out crowd of 15,000 helped celebrate the End Of The Road Festival's 20th birthday this weekend, in one of the final events of the UK summer season.
Britpop luminaries Pulp closed the mainstage on Saturday night at the four-day event, near Blandford Forum, Dorset.
The event's anniversary line-up also included Irish indie-pop singer Cmat, New York art-rockers Geese and Canadian singer-songwriter Mac DeMarco.
More than 140 acts performed across the five music stages which showcased a mix of indie-rock, folk and alternative artists.

articles.title: ‘La Bola Negra’ Fever Hits Telluride: “Let’s Make the Gayest War Movie Ever”
articles.summary: Cannes-winning directors Javier Ambrossi and Javier Calvo joined star Carlos González at an electric post-screening Q&A — capping a weekend of deafening word-of-mouth for the Oscar contender.
body: So Telluride, where La Bola Negra made its North American premiere this weekend, has represented the moment for the movie to prove itself as a true word-of-mouth hit. It’s done that and more. On gondolas and in line for premieres, around cafés and passersby on Colorado Avenue, it’s among the films I’ve heard about the most — a sweeping emotional experience that doubles as a deftly ambitious and subversive exploration of Spanish queer history.

The filmmakers, alongside star Carlos González, gathered on Sunday for a post-screening Q&A (moderated by yours truly) at the Palm Theater on the town’s western edge, where they met an electric response. As Calvo summed up the grand vision behind the movie: “Let’s give all the straight people the war movie they want, but let’s give our community the love story that they want — why can’t we have it all?”
